author: Mozart
title: The catalogue and the duet
about: Mozart’s opera to Lorenzo Da Ponte’s Italian words was first given in Prague in 1787. In Act 1 Don Giovanni slips away from Donna Elvira, a lady he has deserted, and leaves his servant Leporello to tell her everything. Leporello reads to her from the list he keeps of his master’s women. Later the Don comes upon a peasant wedding, sends the others off, tells the bride, Zerlina, that he will marry her at once in a small country house of his, and begins the duet.

view.says: Auden reads the Don as a man with one end, chosen at will: to seduce all the women there are. He sets him against the Duke in Verdi’s *Rigoletto*, a libertine of the senses, who goes after any pretty girl and turns his eyes from a plain, older woman. The Don’s looks should tell the audience nothing, and stamps would have done as well as women. He can be understood only together with Leporello.
view.quote: not sensual but arithmetical; his satisfaction lies in adding one more name to his list which is kept for him by Leporello
view.source: “Balaam and His Ass,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 119–20

lenses.label: Count
lenses.meterName: ten syllables by the Italian count, with the accent fixed on the third, the sixth and the ninth

points.say: The last vowel of the first word and the vowel of the second count as one syllable of the measure. Italian verse counts a vowel that ends one word and a vowel that begins the next in this way, even across a comma, and both vowels are still said. It happens thirteen times in these eight lines.
The verb, *amò*, is stressed on its last syllable, the sixth of the line. The article after it, *il*, begins with a vowel and is counted with that syllable.

The line stops on its last accent, the ninth syllable. Italian names a line by the place of its last accent, so this is still a line of ten. The last line of the count stops the same way, and the two rhyme.
The first accent falls on the country, the second on the hundreds, the third on the last part of the number. The next line is built the same way.
Two countries share this line, and each takes an accent. The hundred that begins the line falls outside the three accents. The last two vowels of the second country are counted as one syllable here.
The second accent falls on the word for already. The thousand follows at once with a stress of its own, off the measure.

lenses.caption: Each line has ten syllables by the Italian count, with the accent on the third, the sixth and the ninth. Two lines stop on the ninth. Italian reference books call this line catchy, its regular cadence monotonous but effective, and its marked rhythm fit for verse to be sung. Da Ponte gives that cadence to a count. In the four lines of totals the first accent always falls on a country and the last on the end of a number. There, only già, already, takes an accent and is neither country nor figure. No woman is named anywhere in the song. Auden calls the Don’s pleasure arithmetical.
lenses.why: The accents of this line never move, and in the totals all but one fall on a country or a figure, so the regular cadence the reference books describe carries a count, and Auden calls the Don’s pleasure arithmetical.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and the whole song for the absence of names. The line of ten syllables and its cadence: Treccani’s *Enciclopedia on line* and the *Enciclopedia Italiana* (1931), under *Decasillabo*. How Italian verse counts syllables and names a line, and this line’s fitness for music: the *Enciclopedia dell’Italiano* (2011), under *Versificazione* and *Sinalefe*. Auden on the Don’s arithmetic: *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 119.

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.caption: Each stanza leaves its first line unrhymed, rhymes its two middle lines and stops short on its last. The two short lines rhyme across the gap: me with tre, me with three. In the first stanza mio, my, ends the line about the master’s loves, and fatt’io, made by me, ends the line about the catalogue. Auden writes that the servant keeps the list and that the Don is never seen to look at it. In the second stanza two totals rhyme because both end in the word for one, and the last total ends on the rhyme for me. The figures appear to be chosen for the verse.
lenses.why: The rhymes fall on the servant’s my and I and on the ends of the totals, and Auden says it is the servant who keeps the list and who alone is seen to enjoy it.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and the lines themselves. Auden on the keeper of the list and on who enjoys it: *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 120. That a line may stop on its accented syllable: the *Enciclopedia dell’Italiano* (2011), under *Versificazione*.

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: It is the pet form of *madama*, a title of respect taken from French, and a servant says it here to a lady of Burgos.
The dictionary also gives it for the book or register that holds such a list.
The adjective for beautiful stands here as a noun, which the dictionary gives for a beautiful woman and for a sweetheart.

Italian can leave the word for *I* unsaid. Here it is said, after the verb, and ends the line. The grammar gives that place as one that brings the subject out, and adds that older writing often put the subject there.
The adverb marks a fact as accomplished, or still being accomplished, at the moment of speaking.

lenses.caption: A catalogo, the dictionary says, is an ordered list of objects of one kind, such as books, works of art or goods. Auden says that stamps would have served the Don as well as women. Leporello calls the women belle, beauties, in the plural. Just before the song he shows Elvira the list and says it is full of their names. He then reads out countries and totals, and not one name. The word già, already, gives the last total as the count so far. Auden writes of the Don Juan of legend that any fondness would make a name of a number on the list.
lenses.why: Leporello says the list is full of names and then reads out totals, and Auden writes that for the Don Juan of legend any fondness would make a name of a number on the list.
lenses.stands: Treccani’s *Vocabolario on line*, under *catalogo*, *bella*, *madama* and *già*, and its *La grammatica italiana*, under *soggetto*. What Leporello says of the list before he reads from it: [Act 1, Scene 5](#/read/don-giovanni/act-1:241), where the English has a large book. The whole song, which names no woman. Auden on stamps, and on numbers and names: *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 119 and 392.

lenses.label: English

ties.say: The English keeps the servant as the maker of the list.
The first Italian stanza ends on this word and the second on its rhyme. The English keeps the word at the end of its line.
Six hundred and forty in the Italian. Seven hundred in the English.
Two hundred and thirty-one in the Italian. The English says eight, or eight hundred if the hundred of the line before is carried over.
A hundred in France and ninety-one in Turkey become ninety-one for the two countries together.
The thousand and three is kept. It still rhymes with the word that ends the first stanza.

lenses.caption: The English beside the Italian appears to be made for singing. Its full lines keep three beats and rhyme on two syllables where they can, and it changes the count. Italy has seven hundred, Germany eight, and France loses its hundred and shares Turkey’s ninety-one. The thousand and three for Spain is kept, with its rhyme. Auden and Chester Kallman, who translated this opera themselves, write that a translation must fit the music as sung, and that such rhymes, mostly comic in English, can help in this song. The Italian figures do not agree either: they come to 2,065, and earlier in the scene Leporello says eighteen hundred.
lenses.why: The English changes the totals and keeps the three beats and the rhymes of two syllables, and Auden and Kallman say a translation must match the rhythm as sung and that such rhymes can help in this song.
lenses.stands: The two texts side by side, and the sum of the five totals on the page. Leporello’s eighteen hundred: [Act 1, Scene 5](#/read/don-giovanni/act-1:177). Auden and Kallman on translating for the voice and on rhymes of two syllables in this song: “Translating Opera Libretti,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 484–85 and 488.

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: The dictionary gives the noun first for conquering by arms and then, in familiar use, for a success in love and for the person won, and it quotes this line and the next.

The dictionary’s first sense is the lively satisfaction of a desire fulfilled; the pleasures of the senses come second. The full form in this Florence printing of 1867 makes the line a syllable too long. The Italian printed with the English libretto clips the word.

notes.gloss: of putting them on the list
notes.note: The noun is a Germanic word for an edge or strip, then a strip of paper, then the sheet that holds a series of names in order.

The noun comes from a Latin verb for suffering and names an intense feeling that can master a person. This printing begins the line with the word for *but*, and the Italian printed with the English with the word for *his*.
The noun names someone at the start of learning an art or a trade. The first word is printed here without the accent that makes it the word for *is*.
The verb comes from French and means to pride oneself on a thing or to insist on a point.
The last word is a diminutive of the word for skirt, which the dictionary says stands in familiar phrases for the woman herself.

notes.gloss: any woman will do for him
notes.note: The verb has here the sense to serve or to be enough. The line is this printing’s own. The Italian printed with the English ends the song on other words, which say that the lady knows what he does.

lenses.caption: The noun conquista, conquest, is a word of war, used also of love. The first two lines give the Don’s reason for winning old women: the piacere, the pleasure, of putting them on the lista, the list. Auden says as much: the Don is satisfied when the list is one name longer. The next two lines name one passion, the young principiante, the beginner. Auden writes that the Don Juan of legend means to be the first man each woman has known. The last lines leave one condition, the gonnella, a skirt, which Italian puts for the woman herself.
lenses.why: Da Ponte puts the pleasure in the listing and the one preference in the beginner, and Auden says the Don is satisfied by one more name and the Don Juan of legend means to be every woman’s first lover.
lenses.stands: Treccani’s *Vocabolario on line* for each word glossed, and its *Thesaurus*, under *conquista*, which quotes four of these lines. Auden on the name added to the list: *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 119. Auden on being each woman’s first lover: “The Greeks and Us,” in *Forewords and Afterwords*, pp. 24–25, where he speaks of the legend of Don Juan and not of this opera.

lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: anaphora
lenses.plain: the same words at the head of clause after clause
lenses.caption: Three clauses in a row begin with the same two words, se sia, whether she is. The figure is anaphora. A different quality follows each time: rich, ugly, beautiful. All three hang on one verb, which says he is not particular, and so make one list of things that do not count. Then Purchè, provided that, brings the one condition, a skirt. Auden quotes these three lines after naming the end the Don has chosen, and says no man so indifferent to looks is met in life. Of the Don Juan of legend he writes that what counts about a woman is only that she belongs to the class of women.
lenses.why: The repeated opening sets rich, ugly and beautiful side by side as things that make no difference, and Auden quotes these lines after naming the Don’s chosen end and says of the legend that only the class of women counts.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. The figure and its definition: *Silva Rhetoricae*, under *anaphora*; for *purché*, Treccani’s *Vocabolario on line*. Auden quotes the three lines in *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 119, and says on p. 121 that no such man is met in life. On the class of women: “The Greeks and Us,” in *Forewords and Afterwords*, p. 24.

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.caption: The first four lines are two couplets, pairs of rhymed lines, and a rhyme that comes back at once makes its two lines one unit. The first couplet rhymes conquista with lista, conquest with list. Leporello has made this rhyme before, asking his master about a new conquest so as to put her on the list. Auden writes that Leporello keeps the list and the Don only tells him the newest name. In the last four lines picca, insists, and ricca, rich, rhyme inside one line, then bella, beautiful, rhymes with gonnella, skirt. The last line stops short and finds its rhyme in an earlier stanza.
lenses.why: A couplet holds its two lines as one unit, so the rhyme binds conquest to list, as it did when Leporello asked his master about a new conquest, and Auden says the Don only tells him the name.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and the rest of the song for the last rhyme. The same two rhyme words come in Leporello’s talk with his master, in English prose at [Act 1, Scene 4](#/read/don-giovanni/act-1:152). The couplet as one unit: Baum’s *Principles of English Versification*, chapter 4; rhyme inside a line: the *Enciclopedia dell’Italiano* (2011), under *Rima*. Auden on the keeper of the list: *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 120.

lenses.label: English

ties.say: The old women of the Italian become *old and young* together, with *high and low* added.
The Italian gives the reason, the pleasure of putting them on the list. The English has no list here. It praises his talk.
The young beginner becomes youth in general.
*Rich* is dropped. *Fat* and *thin* are added, and *short* and *tall* two lines later.
*Ugly* is kept, and *beautiful* becomes *pretty*.
The skirt becomes a petticoat.
This last line is this printing’s own: any woman will do for him. The Italian printed with the English says that the lady knows what he does. The English says he loves them all.

lenses.caption: The English keeps ugly, has pretty for beautiful, and makes the skirt a petticoat. Where the Italian says he wins old women for the pleasure of listing them, the English has no list: it says that old and young own the music of his tongue. Those two Italian lines name what Auden says satisfies the Don: one more name on the list. The English ends on he loves them all. Leporello says loved too, in the second line of the song. Auden, writing of the legend, holds that its Don Juan must give up love, since a woman he cared for at all would be a name and no longer a number.
lenses.why: The English puts praise of the Don’s talk where the Italian has the pleasure of the list, and that couplet is where Da Ponte states the pleasure Auden calls arithmetical.
lenses.stands: The two texts side by side, and the second line of the song, shown in the first passage. The usual last line: the Italian printed with the English in the Metropolitan Opera libretto. Auden on the name added to the list: “Balaam and His Ass,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 119. Auden on love and the legend: “Don Juan,” in the same book, p. 392.

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.caption: The Don’s four lines rhyme by turns, and so do Zerlina’s, on new sounds. Then come four single lines, and each of hers rhymes with his line before it: Masetto answers diletto, beloved, and forte, strong, answers sorte, lot. The last three lines are for both, and their last word, amor, love, takes the rhyme of her cor, heart, and her ancor, yet. Her part goes from a stanza of her own to the answering half of his rhyme to a shared line. Auden, writing of the legend, says the seduction is to be a triumph of the seducer’s will.
lenses.why: Her lines go from a stanza with rhymes of its own to the second halves of his couplets and then to lines shared with him, and Auden says the legend makes the seduction a triumph of the seducer’s will.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and the singers’ names in the Italian. What counts as a rhyme in Italian: the *Enciclopedia dell’Italiano* (2011), under *Rima*. Auden on the seducer’s will: “The Greeks and Us,” in *Forewords and Afterwords*, p. 24, where he speaks of the legend of Don Juan.

lenses.label: Voices
lenses.caption: Six of the Don’s seven verbs are futures, orders or urgings: dirai, you will say, Vieni, come. A future, the reference book says, can carry an order, so all six tell her what is to happen. Three of Zerlina’s eight verbs are conditionals, the mood of a softened wish: Vorrei, I would like. Her other five are presents: her heart trembles, he may fool her, she is no longer strong. This printing puts her stanza in brackets, its mark for words said aside, and in it she speaks of him, not to him. Then both sing his kind of verb, Andiamo, let us go. Auden counts Don Giovanni among opera’s great roles, each a state of passion and will.
lenses.why: Six of the Don’s seven verbs say what will be or what she is to do, hers wish and report, the duet ends on his kind, and Auden calls opera’s great roles, his among them, states of passion and will.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and the brackets this printing sets round words said aside. The verb forms: Treccani’s *Vocabolario on line* and *La grammatica italiana*. The future that commands and the conditional that softens: the *Enciclopedia dell’Italiano* (2010), under *Futuro* and *Condizionale*. Auden on the great roles of opera: “Notes on Music and Opera,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 470.

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: An adverb for a place away from both the speaker and the hearer.
The dictionary says that giving the hand seals a pact, and that to ask for a girl’s hand is to ask to marry her.
The dictionary gives the last word as the one that declares the will to marry, the yes of the bride.
The second word is an adverb for the place where the speaker is.

notes.gloss: I would, and I would not
but he may yet fool me
notes.note: The verb means to make a fool of someone or to deceive, and the last word is the clipped form of the adverb for still or yet.
The dictionary gives the noun for the force that rules human affairs, against which human will can do nothing, and then for what that force deals to each person, whatever the person wills.
The dictionary gives the adverb first for soon, in a short time, and then for quickly, as a word used to urge someone on. The line can be taken either way.
The verb is given in literary use for repairing a harm or making up for a hurt, and the noun for suffering, as in the pains of love.
The adjective is given first for not guilty and then for one who has no experience of evil.

lenses.caption: Just before the duet the Don tells Zerlina he will marry her this instant, in a small country house of his. Each line of his stanza has a word of place: Là, there, twice, then non è lontano, it is not far, then di qui, from here. Giving the hand seals a pact and the yes is a bride’s word, so his first two lines describe a wedding. Zerlina is already a bride. Earlier in the act Donna Elvira says he called her his wife and left her after three days. Auden writes of this Don that one time with a woman is enough for him.
lenses.why: His words of place point to the house where he has said they will marry, hand and yes are wedding words, Elvira says he called her his wife and left, and Auden says one time is enough for this Don.
lenses.stands: Treccani’s *Vocabolario on line* for each word glossed. In the English printed here, where the scene of the duet is numbered 8: what the Don promises just before the duet, [Act 1, Scene 8](#/read/don-giovanni/act-1:351); Zerlina as the bride, [Scene 7](#/read/don-giovanni/act-1:274); what Elvira says he did, [Scene 5](#/read/don-giovanni/act-1:195). Auden on the Don for whom one time is enough: *The Enchafèd Flood*, p. 107.

lenses.label: English

ties.say: The hand is kept.
The yes is kept. The English adds that she will whisper it gently.
The Italian says the place is not far. The English leaves that out and gives her the lord of a castle. Just before the duet the Italian calls the place a small country house.
A heart that trembles a little becomes a breast that heaves with terror.
Her doubt is kept: he may be fooling her.
In the Italian Masetto moves her to pity. In the English he has a claim on her duty, and *duty* rhymes with the last word of the line before.
His word can mean lot or fate. The English gives *state* here and keeps *fate* for her answer, where it makes the rhyme.
In the Italian she says quick, or soon, and that she is no longer strong. In the English she yields to fate.
The Italian goes to make good the pains of an innocent love. The English goes to share a pleasure.

lenses.caption: The English keeps the hand, the yes and Zerlina’s doubt. In the Italian Masetto moves her to pity; in the English he claims my duty. In the Italian she says quick, or soon, and that she is no longer strong; in the English she yields to fate. The Italian word nearest to fate is sorte, and it is his: the lot he says he will change. Each new word answers a rhyme of two syllables: beauty then duty, state, love then fate, love. Auden and Kallman write that such rhymes are mostly comic in English, and that a tender scene is better left unrhymed than rhymed absurdly.
lenses.why: The English gives Zerlina duty and fate where the Italian has pity and failing strength, and both new words are answering rhymes of two syllables, the kind Auden and Kallman call mostly comic in English.
lenses.stands: The two texts side by side. *Pietà*, *presto* and *sorte*: Treccani’s *Vocabolario on line*. The country house, which the English calls only a house: [Act 1, Scene 8](#/read/don-giovanni/act-1:355), as the English numbers it. Auden and Kallman on rhymes of two syllables in English: “Translating Opera Libretti,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 488.

auden.says: When Leporello, in his first song, says he wants to play the gentleman, the audience laughs, Auden notes, because he has nothing of the master about him. By the end, he thinks, the joke turns round, and the servant may have been the master from the start. The list is in Leporello’s keeping, and without it the Don would have no reason for being. The Don is never shown looking at the list or enjoying it. His part is to bring the newest name. Auden also calls him a figure of myth: there are promiscuous men, but none in life to whom the women’s bodies make no difference at all.
auden.source: “Balaam and His Ass,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 118 and 120–21

auden.says: Writing of the legend in general, Auden pairs Don Juan with Tristan and Isolde as two modern myths of love that the Greeks could not have had. What matters to Don Juan about a woman is only that she is one. The list is what makes the myth foreign to the Greeks. He means to be the first man every woman has known, and each is the next number in an endless series. Time is his enemy because it repeats. Auden says both myths are sicknesses that only a Christian imagination could have bred.
auden.source: “The Greeks and Us,” in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), pp. 23–25

auden.says: Auden, writing on Byron’s poem, says it is his will, and no bent of his nature, that makes the Don Juan of legend promiscuous. He has made seduction his calling. Any fondness would make a name of a number on the list, so the calling demands that he give up love. The legend therefore needs him to be a defiant unbeliever, the demonic reverse of the saint who denies himself and prefers no neighbor to another, so that he can be charitable to every one. Byron’s hero has five women in two years, which is little beside the thousand and three in Spain that Leporello reads out.

In *The Enchafèd Flood* Auden puts the Don of Da Ponte and Mozart among the heroes who leave everyone else behind. A seducer looks like a man absorbed in women, and Auden says this one is not. One time is enough for him, and he does not want them to remember him. Some do, and that brings him down. What holds his interest is the tally itself, how many names his private book has reached.
auden.source: *The Enchafèd Flood* (1950; Vintage Books edition, 1967), p. 107

auden.says: Auden quotes Shaw, who sided with Beethoven against Mozart for giving what is glad, tender and noble in him to a libertine in his cups, a foolish peasant girl and a fine lady of the usual kind. Auden answers that Mozart was right, since such feelings are everybody’s. Opera, he says, copies human willfulness: people insist on having their feelings, whatever it costs them. Each great role, Don Giovanni first in his list, is one state of passion and will. In song, he believes, the listener hears syllables and not the words of a poem. For that reason he is in general against performing operas in translation.
auden.source: “Notes on Music and Opera,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 469–70 and 473

auden.says: With Chester Kallman, Auden put the words of this opera into English. They write that a translation has to match the rhythm of the music as sung, which is not the rhythm of the verse as spoken. Italian rhymes mostly on two syllables. English seldom does, and then the effect is usually comic, which in Leporello’s catalogue song can help. A librettist’s own verses, they say, have only to inspire the composer, and before Wagner and the Verdi of the middle years they followed conventions that any able writer of verse could learn.
auden.source: W. H. Auden and Chester Kallman, “Translating Opera Libretti,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 484–85, 488 and 493

auden.says: In June 1941, a few months before the course began, Auden reviewed Denis de Rougemont’s *Love in the Western World*. He says there that the legend of Tristan calls up its reverse, the legend that reaches its height in Mozart’s *Don Giovanni*, where the present moment is everything. For Tristan time is an evil to be endured and for Don Juan an evil to be destroyed, so that the one is like a man who kills himself and the other like a man who kills.
auden.source: “Eros and Agape,” *The Nation*, 28 June 1941; reprinted in his *Prose*, vol. II (2002), pp. 137–40

auden.says: Donald Pearce, who took the course, recalls that at the interview for admission Auden listed some of the authors and added that there would be operas too, in score and libretto: *Carmen*, *Don Giovanni* and *Tristan and Isolde*.
auden.source: Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall: W. H. Auden at Michigan,” in *W. H. Auden: The Far Interior*, edited by Alan Bold (1985), p. 133

sources: The Italian text: Lorenzo Da Ponte’s libretto for Mozart’s *Don Giovanni*, as Italian Wikisource transcribes the printing of Eduardo Ducci (Florence, 1867). The transcription was checked against the copy of that printing at the Internet Archive.

The English text: the unsigned version in the Italian and English libretto that Fred Rullman of New York published for the Metropolitan Opera House, as printed here. Its Italian column was used to check the Florence printing.

W. H. Auden, *The Dyer’s Hand and Other Essays* (1962): “Balaam and His Ass,” pp. 118–21; “Don Juan,” p. 392; “Notes on Music and Opera,” pp. 469–70 and 473; and, with Chester Kallman, “Translating Opera Libretti,” pp. 484–85, 488 and 493.
W. H. Auden, “The Greeks and Us,” in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), pp. 23–25.
W. H. Auden, *The Enchafèd Flood* (1950; Vintage Books edition, 1967), p. 107.

W. H. Auden, “Eros and Agape,” *The Nation*, 28 June 1941, reprinted in his *Prose*, vol. II: 1939–1948, edited by Edward Mendelson (2002), pp. 137–40. Not seen in full: read for this page only in extracts.
Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall: W. H. Auden at Michigan,” in *W. H. Auden: The Far Interior*, edited by Alan Bold (1985), p. 133.
Treccani, *Vocabolario on line* (treccani.it), under each Italian word glossed; *Thesaurus* (2018), under *conquista* and *forte*; *Sinonimi e Contrari* (2003), under *ancora*.

*Enciclopedia dell’Italiano* (Treccani, 2010–11): Claudio Ciociola, “Versificazione” and “Rima”; Sergio Bozzola and Luciano Romito, “Sinalefe”; Elisa De Roberto, “Futuro”; Salvatore Claudio Sgroi, “Condizionale”; Angela Ferrari, “Anafora.”

caveats: The Italian is the Florence printing of 1867 as Italian Wikisource gives it, with its slips, such as *Zar.* for Zerlina. In the second passage one line begins with *but* where the Italian printed with the English has *his*, and the last line is not the one usually sung.

The stanza breaks were made for this page and follow the rhymes. The stresses marked are those of the verse read aloud. In the opera words and lines are repeated, and Auden and Kallman say that the rhythm of verse as sung is not its rhythm as spoken.

Two places in the act go against Auden’s account. Just before the second passage Leporello says his master wants the plump in winter and the thin in summer. Later the Don tells Leporello to add ten names by morning to what he calls his list.

Auden’s sentences on the first lover, the class of women and giving up love are about the legend, not this opera. He held that opera verse before Wagner was a convention, heard as syllables, so the close reading is this page’s own. His 1941 review was read only in extracts.

The English beside the Italian is an unsigned version printed for an opera house. It is free and appears to be made to fit the music. From the wedding on it numbers the scenes one behind the Italian. The first word of Zerlina’s last line can mean quick or soon.
